name: Bimax / double jaw surgery
lead: Bimaxillary ("bimax") surgery, also called double jaw surgery, repositions the upper and lower jaws in one operation. It typically combines a Le Fort I osteotomy of the maxilla with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) of the mandible, and a chin procedure may be added [1]. Because both jaws move, the surgeon can change the bite, the length and projection of the lower face, the position of the chin and the support under the nose and lips together.

It is an established orthognathic procedure used for malocclusion, jaw asymmetry, receding or protruding jaws and obstructive sleep apnea, normally after a period of orthodontic preparation [1]. In looksmaxxing communities the word has become shorthand for the most comprehensive jaw surgery, and members discuss it as a way to reshape facial proportions, with threads weighing it against fillers and implants, braces-only treatment, multi-segment versions and surgery with maxillary skeletal expansion [4][5][6][7].

Published research focuses on bite, airway and quality-of-life outcomes. A 2025 systematic review of 22 cohort studies (1,482 participants) examined what influences quality of life after orthognathic surgery [8], and reviews describe functional and aesthetic benefits alongside the risks of a major operation [1][8].

chain: Upper and lower jaws are cut and moved to planned positions
Bite, jaw projection, chin position and facial proportions change
A different facial profile and lower-face shape
angle.text: Moving both jaws changes the bone framework that the soft tissue of the lower face rests on. Surgeons plan the movements with imaging software that can predict the post-operative face, and members of looksmaxxing communities seek it for profile, recession, underbite or asymmetry changes that other methods do not alter [1].

paras: The Le Fort I cuts and repositions the upper jaw, and the BSSO, developed by Hugo Obwegeser, splits the lower jaw on each side so it can be moved. Both are fixed with plates and screws, and a chin procedure may be added [1]. Wikipedia notes that surgical planning software can predict the post-operative facial shape, which is used to explain the plan to patients [1].

Orthodontic treatment, often with braces, normally precedes surgery for up to about a year so that the teeth sit in a position that allows the jaws to meet correctly afterwards [1]. Looksmaxxing threads on braces before bimax, braces versus bimax and multi-segment techniques reflect this orthodontic stage [5][7].

Orthognathic surgery is performed to correct dentofacial deformities, bite problems, jaw asymmetry and obstructive sleep apnea, and it may also be considered to improve facial aesthetics and self-esteem; because it usually produces a noticeable change in appearance, a psychological assessment is sometimes part of the process [1].

For obstructive sleep apnea, a related two-jaw procedure called maxillomandibular advancement moves both jaws forward. A 2025 meta-analysis compared outcomes across dentofacial classes and reported the largest percentage reduction in the apnoea-hypopnoea index in class I patients [9].
A 2008 systematic review analysed 15 studies on the stability of skeletal Class III (underbite) corrections after double-jaw surgery [10].

According to Wikipedia, initial healing takes 2 to 6 weeks, with bone union and remodelling continuing for a further 2 to 4 months. The jaws are sometimes held together for 1 to 4 weeks, patients usually follow a liquid then soft diet, weight loss is common, and swelling typically fades within weeks although some can last for months [1]. Return to work is possible roughly 2 to 6 weeks after surgery, with recovery rules followed for about 8 weeks [1].

Studies of soft-tissue effects include research on nasolabial changes after double jaw surgery, since moving the maxilla can alter the nose and upper lip [11]. A systematic review and meta-analysis in the European Journal of Orthodontics examined how patient characteristics, procedure type and country development level relate to quality-of-life scores after orthognathic surgery [8].

According to Wikipedia, complications include bleeding, swelling, infection (up to 7% in cited figures) and numbness from inferior alveolar nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months but is rarely permanent [1]. Maxillary impaction is described as riskier than some other movements [1].

A looksmax.org thread on complications of bimax and trimax surgery and a T Nation forum post in which a member describes a failed double jaw surgery with lasting bone loss show that adverse outcomes are also discussed in these communities [12][13].

On looksmax.org, threads ask about cost and recovery, with one poster saying they had heard many people ascend through double jaw surgery and that it is fairly safe, and a reply that price depends on the surgeon [3]. Members in other countries ask whether insurance can cover it for an underbite after seeing social-media accounts of insured patients [2].

Other threads compare bimax with implants, with braces and with multi-segment or MSE variants, and one is titled as arguing that bimax is overrated and overhyped for most people, while others plan it alongside rhinoplasty [4][5][6][7][14]. A T Nation member reported that online peers tell anyone who does not look like a model to get double jaw surgery [15].

Controlled research on orthognathic surgery covers quality of life [8], skeletal stability after double-jaw surgery in Class III malocclusion [10], sleep-apnea outcomes after maxillomandibular advancement [9] and soft-tissue changes in the nasolabial area [11]. Several randomised trials address perioperative care in double-jaw patients, such as pain control and nerve blocks [16][17]. No study has tested the looksmaxxing use of bimax specifically for attractiveness.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known cases of jaw surgery [1].
Osteotomies of the mandible and maxilla are first used [1].
Jaw osteotomies begin to be used for more extreme deformities and TMJ pain [1].
Raffaini introduces orthognathic surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation [1].

lore.intro: Bimax is among the most discussed hardmaxx procedures on looksmax.org, where members compare surgeons, countries, costs and alternatives [2][3][4].

claims.claim: Double jaw surgery makes people "ascend" and is decently safe.
claims.believers: A poster says many people ascend through it and that it is reasonably safe [3].
claims.experts: Reviews report functional and aesthetic benefit and quality-of-life gains, alongside documented risks including infection, bleeding and nerve numbness [1][8].

claims.claim: Bimax can be obtained cheaply or free through insurance for an underbite.
claims.believers: A poster cites a social-media account of an insured patient with an underbite and asks how to do the same [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes surgery as treatment for dentofacial deformity and malocclusion; coverage rules vary by insurer and country and are not described there [1].

claims.claim: Bimax is overrated and overhyped for most people.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues that most people would not gain much from the operation [14].
claims.experts: Studies examine functional and quality-of-life outcomes rather than attractiveness gains for people without a bite or skeletal problem [8].

claims.claim: Implants or braces may achieve similar looks with less surgery.
claims.believers: Threads compare bimax with implants and with braces as alternatives [5][6].
claims.experts: Orthodontics alone does not move the skeletal jaws, whereas orthognathic surgery repositions them [1].

card.summary: Forum shorthand for surgery that repositions both the upper and lower jaw at once; an established orthognathic procedure with documented functional benefits and real surgical risks.
card.aka: Bimaxillary surgery, double jaw surgery, bimax, Le Fort I plus BSSO
card.note: Evidence is for bite and airway outcomes; recovery involves weeks of restrictions, and nerve numbness and infection are documented risks.

quick.overview:
Bimax, or double jaw surgery, means operating on both jaws in one procedure, typically a Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw and a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw. It is used for dentofacial deformities, bite problems, airway obstruction and facial disproportion.

Looksmaxxing communities treat it as a major hardmaxx option for changing facial structure. Surgeons usually combine it with orthodontic treatment before and after the operation.
quick.mechanism: The upper and lower jaw bones are cut and moved into new positions, then held with plates and screws while they heal. Wikipedia says infection rates up to 7% are reported and that nerve numbness is usually temporary.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months but is rarely permanent. Full bone healing takes months, and diet is liquid for a time. Surgery is performed by oral and maxillofacial or plastic surgeons.
